architectural_implications.after: Explicit runtime layer: sandboxed execution plus session store plus rehydration contract, managed as its own concern.
architectural_implications.before: Stateless request/response handlers; state lives in an external database accessed ad hoc by application code.
architectural_implications.consequence: New owned component (rehydration and session persistence), new failure modes (stale or partially restored state), and a durability/resume requirement on every tool-using agent.
architectural_implications.observation: State lifecycle for agents is being split out of the execution environment into a distinct persisted-state plus rehydration layer, with custom implementations where platform runtimes fall short.

architectural_implications.after: Short-term, long-term, and episodic tiers with ingestion and consolidation pipelines feeding each.
architectural_implications.before: RAG index plus top-k retrieval stuffed into the prompt.
architectural_implications.consequence: Memory gains data-engineering costs (pipelines, consolidation jobs, tier promotion rules) and its own correctness/freshness SLOs, moving it onto the data platform roadmap.
architectural_implications.observation: Memory is reclassified from a retrieval concern to a tiered storage-and-consolidation subsystem.

architectural_implications.after: OTEL spans per reasoning step and tool call, with trajectory-level evals.
architectural_implications.before: Log lines and final-response inspection; evals on answer correctness.
architectural_implications.consequence: Trace schema becomes an interface other teams and vendors depend on, and cost/storage scales with reasoning steps rather than requests.
architectural_implications.observation: Observability moves from output logging to structured trajectory tracing including belief state and tool-call confidence.

architectural_implications.after: Dynamically loaded skill bundles assembled per task phase via progressive disclosure.
architectural_implications.before: One large system prompt with all tool definitions and domain instructions resident.
architectural_implications.consequence: Skill loading becomes a latency and correctness path (a mis-loaded skill silently degrades output), and skills become versioned, independently testable artifacts.
architectural_implications.observation: Capability packaging becomes the context boundary: a skill = instructions + domain setup + tools, loaded on demand.

article_ideas.angle: Walk the microservices analogy forward: 2015 teams expected containers to solve orchestration and had to build service mesh and lifecycle management themselves; 2026 teams are making the identical bet on agent runtimes, and the missing layer is state.
article_ideas.audience: Platform and infrastructure engineers deploying agents in regulated enterprises
article_ideas.based_on: Enterprise requirements demand custom solutions where cloud providers fall short.
article_ideas.thesis: Managed agent runtimes supply the sandbox but not the state lifecycle, so the rehydration layer belongs in your architecture diagram from day one — teams that treat session persistence as a platform feature end up maintaining an undocumented workaround that only fails in production.
article_ideas.title: Your Agent Runtime Leaks: Rehydration Is Your Component, Not Your Cloud's

article_ideas.angle: Reframe the design question from 'what do we retrieve?' to 'what do we persist, when do we consolidate, and which tier does a fact graduate to?' and show why naive RAG has no answer to any of the three.
article_ideas.audience: Data platform and applied AI engineers who own retrieval infrastructure
article_ideas.based_on: Memory is not just retrieval; agents need persistent and evolving state across sessions.
article_ideas.thesis: Treating memory as retrieval caps an agent at statelessness with extra steps; the work that actually makes memory function is write paths, consolidation jobs, and tier promotion policies — a data-platform concern with its own freshness and correctness SLOs.
article_ideas.title: Agent Memory Is an ETL Problem, Not a Prompting Problem

article_ideas.angle: Argue from diagnosability: show that output-level checks are structurally blind to belief-level errors, then specify the minimum span fields that make a failed run reconstructable after the fact.
article_ideas.based_on: Traditional logging is insufficient for agents due to high volume of internal reasoning.
article_ideas.thesis: Final-output evals and log tailing cannot diagnose non-deterministic agent failures because the failure frequently lives in a wrong intermediate belief; trace schemas carrying reasoning steps and tool-call confidence are the real prerequisite for trajectory evaluation, not an optional vendor add-on.
article_ideas.title: Instrument the Belief, Not the Answer

article_ideas.angle: Invert the prevailing orchestrator-plus-specialists tutorial pattern; require a stated boundary justification before decomposition, and show what that justification looks like in practice.
article_ideas.audience: Staff-plus engineers and architects designing agent systems
article_ideas.based_on: Start with single agents with subskills before adopting complex multi-agent setups.
article_ideas.thesis: Multi-agent decomposition should be treated as a cost, not a default starting architecture: each hop adds a lossy interface and another failure domain, so the burden of proof for splitting must be an isolation or ownership requirement, exactly as it should have been for microservices.
article_ideas.title: Start With the Agent Monolith — and Make Splitting Expensive to Justify

article_ideas.angle: Apply the service-to-service auth playbook (scoped tokens, identity providers) to non-human agent principals coordinating over MCP and A2A.
article_ideas.audience: Security architects and platform engineers shipping tool-using agents
article_ideas.based_on: Agents act on behalf of users, blurring authorization boundaries.
article_ideas.thesis: Agents acting on a user's behalf break inherited authorization, so identity, scoped credentials, and permission must be modeled explicitly at the tool-execution boundary — prompt-level guardrails are not an authorization mechanism.
article_ideas.title: The Agent Is a Principal: Delegated Authority Without Silent Escalation

connections.connects_to: microservices durability and orchestration (service mesh, container orchestration)
connections.relationship: Historical analogy: the missing platform layer in 2015 microservices (orchestration, mesh) parallels the missing state/session layer for agents now.

connections.connects_to: context window budget and token cost
connections.relationship: Loading skill bundles on demand is a direct mechanism for trading context-assembly complexity for lower token usage and higher focus.
Traces are the substrate that trajectory evaluation consumes; better span semantics enable better non-deterministic evaluation.

connections.concept: agents acting on behalf of users
connections.connects_to: scoped credentials, least privilege, MCP and A2A
connections.relationship: Delegated authority requires explicit principal modeling and protocol-level trust between agents.

connections.connects_to: single agent with subskills before multi-agent
connections.relationship: Same architectural discipline applied to a new substrate: prove the cohesive unit before distributing it.

evidence_quotes.text: Agents are stateful by necessity, requiring sandboxed isolation and session persistence.
Agents are stateful by necessity
Enterprise requirements demand custom solutions where cloud providers fall short.

core_insights.generalization: Any long-running, stateful compute abstraction (workflow engines, durable execution, actor models) must separate the execution sandbox from the persisted state and define an explicit rehydration contract; otherwise platform abstractions leak and teams rebuild the same layer.
core_insights.insight: Agents break the stateless-execution assumption that cloud API infrastructure is built on: they require sandboxed isolation, session persistence, lifecycle management, and explicit rehydration of state between invocations. Navan reportedly had to build custom rehydration layers on top of provider agent runtimes (AWS Agent Core, Azure preview) because enterprise requirements exceeded what the runtimes supplied.
core_insights.why_it_matters: If state lifecycle is treated as an infrastructure detail rather than a first-class architectural layer, the failure modes appear only in production — lost session context, unsafe cross-tenant sandbox leakage, and un-resumable long-running tasks. Rehydration logic becomes a custom component you own, not something you inherit.

evidence_quotes.text: Memory is not just retrieval; agents need persistent and evolving state across sessions.
AgentCore memory implementation combined with custom ingestion pipelines.
Engineers must build ingestion and consolidation pipelines for agent memory.

core_insights.generalization: For any agent expected to act consistently across sessions, the design question shifts from 'what do we retrieve?' to 'what do we persist, when do we consolidate, and which tier does a fact graduate to?' — an ETL problem more than a prompting problem.
core_insights.insight: Memory is treated as a state-management subsystem with tiers (short-term, long-term, episodic) plus its own ingestion and consolidation pipelines — distinct from retrieval. RAG is positioned as a retrieval mechanism, insufficient as a memory architecture.
core_insights.why_it_matters: This relocates memory from a prompt-construction concern to a data-pipeline concern: you need write paths, consolidation/summarization jobs, and tier promotion policies, not just an embedding index and a top-k query. It also implies memory has its own freshness and correctness failure modes.

evidence_quotes.text: Traditional logging is insufficient for agents due to high volume of internal reasoning.
Using OTEL traces with specialized providers like Braintrust.
Traditional log tailing does not capture agent belief states, reasoning chains, and tool call confidence.

core_insights.generalization: As systems become non-deterministic, observability must move up from 'what happened at the I/O boundary' to 'what did the system believe and why' — the trace schema becomes part of the system contract, not a vendor add-on.
core_insights.insight: Agent observability requires capturing internal intent — belief states, reasoning chains, and tool-call confidence — as structured execution traces (OTEL spans, via a provider like Braintrust), because raw log tailing cannot represent the volume and structure of internal reasoning. Evaluation then operates on trajectories rather than final outputs.
core_insights.why_it_matters: This defines a concrete instrumentation surface: spans per reasoning step and tool call with confidence metadata, enabling trajectory-level evals and post-hoc debugging of non-deterministic runs. Without it, a failed agent run is un-diagnosable because the failure may be a wrong intermediate belief rather than a wrong answer.

evidence_quotes.text: Skills as units of context, combining instructions, domain setup, and tool execution.
Progressive disclosure prevents context window overload and loss of focus.
Modular tools like booking and payment skills loaded dynamically.

core_insights.generalization: Context should be assembled like a build artifact with dependency boundaries per capability, rather than a static prompt; the capability boundary and the context boundary should be the same boundary.
core_insights.insight: Skills are proposed as the unit of context — bundling instructions, domain setup, and tool execution — and are loaded dynamically via 'progressive disclosure' so that only the relevant skill's context occupies the window at any moment.
core_insights.why_it_matters: This is a concrete context-economy mechanism: instead of one global prompt plus every tool definition, context is composed per task phase. It makes context a versioned, composable artifact and gives an explicit lever for token cost and focus degradation.

evidence_quotes.text: If you can't build a well-structured monolith, what makes you think microservices is the answer?
Start with single agents with subskills before adopting complex multi-agent setups.
Prevents runaway agent behavior and cascading hallucinations in enterprise AI.

core_insights.generalization: Distributed decomposition of non-deterministic components multiplies error propagation paths; the burden of proof should be on splitting, exactly as with services, because each boundary adds a lossy interface and a new failure domain.
core_insights.insight: Rather than starting with multi-agent networks, start with a single agent exposing subskills; multi-agent topologies are a scaling step, not a starting architecture. The stated rationale is avoiding cascading failures (and, by analogy, cascading hallucinations) across agent hops.
core_insights.why_it_matters: This directly counters the default 'orchestrator plus specialists' starting point and reframes multi-agent decomposition as a cost to be justified by a required isolation or ownership boundary. It also collapses two abstractions (agent and skill) early, keeping the debug surface small.

evidence_quotes.text: Agents act on behalf of users, blurring authorization boundaries.
Establish strict guardrails and scoped credentials for tool execution.

core_insights.generalization: Whenever a non-human component acts with delegated authority, the system needs explicit delegation and scoping semantics — the same problem service-to-service auth solved with scoped tokens and identity providers.
core_insights.insight: Agents acting on behalf of users blur the authorization boundary: the agent is a distinct principal holding scoped credentials and least-privilege grants, running tools over MCP and coordinating over A2A, so identity and permission must be modeled explicitly rather than inherited implicitly from the calling user.
core_insights.why_it_matters: This makes credential scoping and inter-agent protocol trust a first-class design element, and it means guardrails must sit at the tool-execution boundary where authority is actually exercised. Without delegation semantics, permission escalation is silent.

evidence_quotes.text: Agents are stateful by necessity, requiring sandboxed isolation and session persistence.
Cloud providers offering agent runtimes (AWS Agent Core, Azure preview).
Transitioning from stateless API execution environments to stateful agent runtimes.

deep_dives.research_question: Which enterprise constraints (session length, resume-after-failure semantics, multi-tenant sandbox isolation, data residency) are already satisfied by managed agent runtimes such as AWS Agent Core and Azure preview, and which force a custom rehydration layer — and can that boundary be expressed as an explicit, testable contract?
deep_dives.topic: The runtime/rehydration boundary between platform agent runtimes and application-owned state
deep_dives.trigger_insight: Enterprise requirements demand custom solutions where cloud providers fall short.
deep_dives.why: If the split is left implicit, every team discovers the missing piece in production via lost session context, non-resumable long-running tasks, or cross-tenant sandbox leakage. Making the rehydration contract a documented interface turns a bespoke workaround into a shippable component and lets teams compare managed runtimes on the axis that actually matters.

evidence_quotes.text: Moving beyond naive RAG to comprehensive short-term, long-term, and episodic memory systems.
AgentCore memory implementation combined with custom ingestion pipelines.
Enables agents to maintain context and learn from past interactions.

deep_dives.research_question: Do short-term / long-term / episodic memory tiers with explicit consolidation and promotion policies measurably outperform a well-tuned retrieval index on multi-session task success, and at what ingestion and maintenance cost?
deep_dives.topic: Memory as a tiered data pipeline: ingestion, consolidation, and tier promotion
deep_dives.trigger_insight: Memory is not just retrieval; agents need persistent and evolving state across sessions.
deep_dives.why: This relocates memory from prompt construction to data engineering: write paths, summarization jobs, freshness rules, and per-tier correctness failure modes. Without this, 'agent memory' quietly becomes an embedding index with no defined semantics for what persists, when it is consolidated, or when a fact graduates between tiers.

evidence_quotes.text: Using Braintrust to emit hotel traces and capture execution spans.
Critical for debugging and ensuring production reliability.
Addressing the non-deterministic nature of agents through execution traces and trajectory evals.

deep_dives.research_question: What proportion of real agent production incidents are diagnosable from input/output logs alone versus requiring intermediate reasoning spans, belief status, and tool-call confidence — and which minimum span fields close the gap?
deep_dives.topic: A trace schema that carries belief state, not just I/O
deep_dives.trigger_insight: Traditional logging is insufficient for agents due to high volume of internal reasoning.
deep_dives.why: Non-deterministic failures often originate in a wrong intermediate belief rather than a wrong final answer, so an I/O-only log leaves the run un-diagnosable. Answering this quantitatively converts 'agents need better observability' into a minimum viable span schema that instrumentation providers and eval pipelines can share.

evidence_quotes.text: Skills as units of context, combining instructions, domain setup, and tool execution.
Modular tools like booking and payment skills loaded dynamically.
Optimizes token usage and execution accuracy.

deep_dives.research_question: Holding model and tool set constant, does per-phase dynamic skill loading improve task accuracy and reduce token cost versus a single resident prompt — and how often does the loader select the wrong or incomplete skill bundle, and at what accuracy penalty?
deep_dives.topic: Progressive disclosure as a context-assembly correctness problem
deep_dives.trigger_insight: Progressive disclosure prevents context window overload and loss of focus.
deep_dives.why: Progressive disclosure is presented only as a win, but it inserts a decision point that can silently degrade output and adds latency. Quantifying both the upside and the misfire rate turns context economy into an engineering budget rather than an assumption.

evidence_quotes.text: Prevents runaway agent behavior and cascading hallucinations in enterprise AI.
If you can't build a well-structured monolith, what makes you think microservices is the answer?
Building multi-agent systems without a well-structured monolith equivalent fails.

deep_dives.research_question: On a fixed task suite, how do error propagation rate, context pressure, and per-task cost scale with the number of agent hops, and what measurable signal justifies the first split?
deep_dives.topic: The decomposition threshold: single agent with subskills versus multi-agent
deep_dives.trigger_insight: Start with single agents with subskills before adopting complex multi-agent setups.
deep_dives.why: The recommendation to start single-agent is stated as principle, not threshold. Without a measured error-propagation curve, 'start monolithic' is unfalsifiable advice that either blocks legitimate scaling or gets ignored entirely.

key_claims.evidence: Trajectory evals are necessary to evaluate multi-step agent success.

open_questions.question: How do we establish deterministic testing for non-deterministic agents?
open_questions.research_direction: Build replayable trajectory fixtures from recorded traces, seed-controlled tool mocks, and trajectory-level assertions (ordering and tool-choice invariants) as the unit of regression testing.
open_questions.why_unresolved: The summary lists this as an open question for investigation; the proposed answer space (execution traces, trajectory evals) captures behavior but does not by itself create reproducible test conditions.

open_questions.question: What standardized trace format will the industry converge upon?
open_questions.research_direction: Compare candidate span semantics for agent reasoning (tool call, belief state, confidence) across instrumentation providers and test portability of the same trace across two backends.
open_questions.why_unresolved: The speakers indicate agents need belief/reasoning/tool-confidence spans but that no converged schema exists; OTEL is used as transport with provider-specific extensions.

open_questions.question: Where does the boundary belong between platform-provided agent runtime and application-owned rehydration/state logic?
open_questions.research_direction: Enumerate enterprise constraints (residency, long-running sessions, resume-after-failure, multi-tenant isolation) and measure which managed runtimes already satisfy them.
open_questions.why_unresolved: The summary reports Navan building custom rehydration layers because enterprise requirements exceeded cloud runtimes, but does not define which requirements are the trigger.

open_questions.question: When is multi-agent decomposition justified over a single agent with subskills?
open_questions.research_direction: Benchmark the same task suite as a single agent with skills versus a multi-agent split, measuring error propagation rate, context pressure, and per-task cost.
open_questions.why_unresolved: The summary recommends starting single-agent to avoid cascading failures but does not specify the threshold at which splitting becomes correct.

project_ideas.based_on: Agents are stateful by necessity, requiring sandboxed isolation and session persistence.
project_ideas.hypothesis: A declared rehydration contract (session snapshot shape, resume semantics, isolation guarantees) can be tested against at least two managed agent runtimes, and each will fail a measurable subset of enterprise constraints — resume-after-crash, session length beyond a threshold, multi-tenant sandbox isolation — forcing an application-owned layer.
project_ideas.measurement: Fraction of interrupted sessions resumed correctly per runtime; number of custom lines of rehydration code required; count of enterprise constraints satisfied out of the enumerated matrix; latency overhead of the rehydration step.
project_ideas.name: Rehydration Conformance Harness
project_ideas.poc: Build a long-running tool-using agent, run it on AWS Agent Core and an Azure agent runtime, kill the process mid-task across a matrix of session lengths and tenant configurations, and score each runtime on how much state it restores versus how much must be re-supplied by a custom rehydration component.

project_ideas.based_on: Memory is not just retrieval; agents need persistent and evolving state across sessions.
project_ideas.hypothesis: On multi-session tasks, a tiered memory system with explicit consolidation and promotion policies beats a well-tuned flat retrieval index on task success, but the gain is smaller than the added ingestion and maintenance cost suggests, and gains concentrate in tasks requiring cross-session consistency rather than single-session recall.
project_ideas.measurement: Cross-session task success rate; stale-fact retrieval rate; token cost per session; wall-clock and dollar cost of consolidation jobs per thousand interactions.
project_ideas.name: Memory Tier Ablation Bench
project_ideas.poc: Implement one agent against three memory backends behind a common interface — flat RAG, tiered short/long/episodic with a nightly consolidation job, and tiered plus episodic summarization — and run an identical multi-session task suite against each with fixed ingestion pipelines.

project_ideas.based_on: Traditional logging is insufficient for agents due to high volume of internal reasoning.
project_ideas.hypothesis: Trajectory-level traces with reasoning spans, belief status, and tool-call confidence make diagnosable a substantial share of agent production incidents that I/O-only logs cannot explain, and a minimal span schema (reasoning step, tool call, confidence) captures most of that gain.
project_ideas.measurement: Root-cause identification accuracy and time-to-diagnosis per instrumentation level; fraction of fault classes undiagnosable at each level; trace storage volume and cost per reasoning step versus per request.
project_ideas.name: Belief-Span Diagnosability Study
project_ideas.poc: Inject a fixed catalog of faults into a tool-using agent (wrong intermediate belief, wrong tool selection, low-confidence tool call, stale memory), run with three instrumentation levels — plain logs, OTEL spans without belief fields, OTEL spans with belief and confidence fields — and have engineers attempt root-cause identification blind to the injected fault.

project_ideas.based_on: Establish strict guardrails and scoped credentials for tool execution.
project_ideas.hypothesis: Enforcing least-privilege scoped credentials at the tool-execution boundary blocks authority-escalation attempts that prompt-level guardrails permit, and this holds across both MCP tool calls and agent-to-agent handoffs where the delegated scope must narrow rather than persist.
project_ideas.measurement: Escalation attempts blocked versus allowed per configuration; false-denial rate on legitimate tasks; added latency per tool call; number of scopes correctly narrowed across A2A hops.
project_ideas.name: Scoped Delegation Gate
project_ideas.poc: Build a gateway in front of agent tool calls that issues short-lived scoped credentials per skill invocation and validates scope at execution time; run a red-team suite of escalation attempts (over-broad tool invocation, scope reuse across hops, prompt-injected instruction to act beyond user intent) against prompt-only guardrails versus the gateway.

summary.html:
Overview

  • Speaker: Roberto Milev & Uday Kanagala
  • Channel: AI Engineer
  • Main topic: AI Agent Architecture and Enterprise Adoption Challenges
  • Purpose: To provide an architectural reference framework for building production-ready AI agents in enterprises by drawing parallels from the microservices evolution. Roberto Milev and Uday Kanagala from Navan compare the current state of AI agent development to the microservices boom of 2015, highlighting recurring architectural patterns, challenges, and missing components in production systems.

Topic Map

Introduction and Analogy to Microservices

  • Explanation: Comparing AI agent adoption pitfalls to the microservices hype cycle of 2015.
  • Key claims:
    • Industry cycles repeat paradigm shifts.
    • Building multi-agent systems without a well-structured monolith equivalent fails.
  • Examples:
    • Microservices adoption led to service mesh and container orchestration over time.
  • Terminology:
    • monolith
    • microservices
    • agentic loop
  • Why it matters: Helps engineers avoid repeating historical architectural mistakes when adopting AI agents.

Runtime Layer & Stateless vs. Stateful

  • Explanation: Transitioning from stateless API execution environments to stateful agent runtimes.
  • Key claims:
    • Agents are stateful by necessity, requiring sandboxed isolation and session persistence.
  • Examples:
    • Cloud providers offering agent runtimes (AWS Agent Core, Azure preview).
  • Terminology:
    • sandboxed isolation
    • session persistence
    • lifecycle management
  • Why it matters: Proper runtime architecture is foundational for scalable enterprise agent deployment.

Memory Management in Agents

  • Explanation: Moving beyond naive RAG to comprehensive short-term, long-term, and episodic memory systems.
  • Key claims:
    • Memory is not just retrieval; agents need persistent and evolving state across sessions.
  • Examples:
    • AgentCore memory implementation combined with custom ingestion pipelines.
  • Terminology:
    • RAG
    • episodic memory
    • long-term memory
  • Why it matters: Enables agents to maintain context and learn from past interactions.

Skills & Context Management

  • Explanation: Skills as units of context, combining instructions, domain setup, and tool execution.
  • Key claims:
    • Progressive disclosure prevents context window overload and loss of focus.
  • Examples:
    • Modular tools like booking and payment skills loaded dynamically.
  • Terminology:
    • progressive disclosure
    • context window
    • structured prompting
  • Why it matters: Optimizes token usage and execution accuracy.

Observability and Testing

  • Explanation: Addressing the non-deterministic nature of agents through execution traces and trajectory evals.
  • Key claims:
    • Traditional logging is insufficient for agents due to high volume of internal reasoning.
  • Examples:
    • Using Braintrust to emit hotel traces and capture execution spans.
  • Terminology:
    • execution traces
    • trajectory evals
    • belief status
  • Why it matters: Critical for debugging and ensuring production reliability.

Guardrails, Authorization, and Single vs. Multi-Agent

  • Explanation: Managing security, scoped credentials, and inter-agent communication protocols.
  • Key claims:
    • Agents act on behalf of users, blurring authorization boundaries.
    • Start with single agents with subskills before adopting complex multi-agent setups.
  • Examples:
    • Model Context Protocol (MCP) and Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocols.
  • Terminology:
    • scoped credentials
    • least privilege
    • A2A protocol
  • Why it matters: Prevents runaway agent behavior and cascading hallucinations in enterprise AI.

Key Points

Agents are stateful by necessity

  • Explanation: Unlike stateless API microservices, agents require session persistence, sandboxed isolation, and rehydration.
  • Evidence: Cloud providers building agent-specific runtime environments.
  • Practical implication: Architectures must account for long-running state and secure session storage.

Memory extends beyond RAG

  • Explanation: Retrieval-augmented generation is insufficient for agents that must remember historical interactions and decisions.
  • Evidence: Implementation of short-term, long-term, and episodic memory tiers.
  • Practical implication: Engineers must build ingestion and consolidation pipelines for agent memory.

Observability requires intent and reasoning tracing

  • Explanation: Traditional log tailing does not capture agent belief states, reasoning chains, and tool call confidence.
  • Evidence: Using OTEL traces with specialized providers like Braintrust.
  • Practical implication: Teams need new tooling to debug non-deterministic agent executions.

Frameworks, Models & Processes

AI Agent Reference Architecture

  • How it works: A layered model for organizing enterprise agent systems from runtime up to orchestration.
  • Components:
    • Runtime
    • Memory
    • Skills & Context
    • Observability
    • Testing
    • Guardrails
    • Orchestration
  • When to use: When designing enterprise-grade AI agent systems.

Examples & Case Studies

Navan adopting cloud runtime environments and building custom rehydration layers.

  • Illustrates: Bridging the gap between stateless cloud infrastructure and stateful agent requirements.
  • Lesson: Enterprise requirements demand custom solutions where cloud providers fall short.

Actionable Takeaways

  • Immediate:
    • Adopt progressive disclosure for context management.
    • Implement OTEL tracing for agent tool calls and reasoning chains.
  • Strategic:
    • Start with single-agent architectures with subskills before moving to multi-agent networks.
    • Establish strict guardrails and scoped credentials for tool execution.
  • Questions to investigate:
    • How do we establish deterministic testing for non-deterministic agents?
    • What standardized trace format will the industry converge upon?

Claims Worth Verifying

  • Model Context Protocol (MCP) has emerged as a de facto protocol for tool calling. (industry trend)
  • Trajectory evals are necessary to evaluate multi-step agent success. (architectural best practice)

Notable Quotes

"If you can't build a well-structured monolith, what makes you think microservices is the answer?" (at 0:40) "We know what's needed. Most of it exists. Go build the rest." (at 31:42)

Compressed Summary

  • Agents mirror microservices in 2015 by facing maturity, observability, and testing challenges.
  • A reference architecture spans runtime, memory, skills, observability, testing, guardrails, and orchestration.
  • Memory is not just retrieval; it requires multi-tiered short-term, long-term, and episodic storage.
  • Single agents with subskills are recommended over complex multi-agent setups initially to avoid cascading failures.
  • Keywords: agents, microservices, architecture, observability, memory
  • Core insight: AI agents are currently experiencing the same architectural growing pains as microservices in 2015, requiring disciplined layering in runtime, memory, observability, and guardrails to succeed in enterprise production.

## Overview
- **Speaker**: Roberto Milev & Uday Kanagala
- **Channel**: AI Engineer
- **Main topic**: AI Agent Architecture and Enterprise Adoption Challenges
- **Purpose**: To provide an architectural reference framework for building production-ready AI agents in enterprises by drawing parallels from the microservices evolution.
Roberto Milev and Uday Kanagala from Navan compare the current state of AI agent development to the microservices boom of 2015, highlighting recurring architectural patterns, challenges, and missing components in production systems.
## Topic Map
### Introduction and Analogy to Microservices
- **Explanation**: Comparing AI agent adoption pitfalls to the microservices hype cycle of 2015.
- **Key claims**:
  - Industry cycles repeat paradigm shifts.
  - Building multi-agent systems without a well-structured monolith equivalent fails.
- **Examples**:
  - Microservices adoption led to service mesh and container orchestration over time.
- **Terminology**:
  - monolith
  - microservices
  - agentic loop
- **Why it matters**: Helps engineers avoid repeating historical architectural mistakes when adopting AI agents.
### Runtime Layer & Stateless vs. Stateful
- **Explanation**: Transitioning from stateless API execution environments to stateful agent runtimes.
- **Key claims**:
  - Agents are stateful by necessity, requiring sandboxed isolation and session persistence.
- **Examples**:
  - Cloud providers offering agent runtimes (AWS Agent Core, Azure preview).
- **Terminology**:
  - sandboxed isolation
  - session persistence
  - lifecycle management
- **Why it matters**: Proper runtime architecture is foundational for scalable enterprise agent deployment.
### Memory Management in Agents
- **Explanation**: Moving beyond naive RAG to comprehensive short-term, long-term, and episodic memory systems.
- **Key claims**:
  - Memory is not just retrieval; agents need persistent and evolving state across sessions.
- **Examples**:
  - AgentCore memory implementation combined with custom ingestion pipelines.
- **Terminology**:
  - RAG
  - episodic memory
  - long-term memory
- **Why it matters**: Enables agents to maintain context and learn from past interactions.
### Skills & Context Management
- **Explanation**: Skills as units of context, combining instructions, domain setup, and tool execution.
- **Key claims**:
  - Progressive disclosure prevents context window overload and loss of focus.
- **Examples**:
  - Modular tools like booking and payment skills loaded dynamically.
- **Terminology**:
  - progressive disclosure
  - context window
  - structured prompting
- **Why it matters**: Optimizes token usage and execution accuracy.
### Observability and Testing
- **Explanation**: Addressing the non-deterministic nature of agents through execution traces and trajectory evals.
- **Key claims**:
  - Traditional logging is insufficient for agents due to high volume of internal reasoning.
- **Examples**:
  - Using Braintrust to emit hotel traces and capture execution spans.
- **Terminology**:
  - execution traces
  - trajectory evals
  - belief status
- **Why it matters**: Critical for debugging and ensuring production reliability.
### Guardrails, Authorization, and Single vs. Multi-Agent
- **Explanation**: Managing security, scoped credentials, and inter-agent communication protocols.
- **Key claims**:
  - Agents act on behalf of users, blurring authorization boundaries.
  - Start with single agents with subskills before adopting complex multi-agent setups.
- **Examples**:
  - Model Context Protocol (MCP) and Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocols.
- **Terminology**:
  - scoped credentials
  - least privilege
  - A2A protocol
- **Why it matters**: Prevents runaway agent behavior and cascading hallucinations in enterprise AI.
## Key Points
### Agents are stateful by necessity
- **Explanation**: Unlike stateless API microservices, agents require session persistence, sandboxed isolation, and rehydration.
- **Evidence**: Cloud providers building agent-specific runtime environments.
- **Practical implication**: Architectures must account for long-running state and secure session storage.
### Memory extends beyond RAG
- **Explanation**: Retrieval-augmented generation is insufficient for agents that must remember historical interactions and decisions.
- **Evidence**: Implementation of short-term, long-term, and episodic memory tiers.
- **Practical implication**: Engineers must build ingestion and consolidation pipelines for agent memory.
### Observability requires intent and reasoning tracing
- **Explanation**: Traditional log tailing does not capture agent belief states, reasoning chains, and tool call confidence.
- **Evidence**: Using OTEL traces with specialized providers like Braintrust.
- **Practical implication**: Teams need new tooling to debug non-deterministic agent executions.
## Frameworks, Models & Processes
### AI Agent Reference Architecture
- **How it works**: A layered model for organizing enterprise agent systems from runtime up to orchestration.
- **Components**:
  - Runtime
  - Memory
  - Skills & Context
  - Observability
  - Testing
  - Guardrails
  - Orchestration
- **When to use**: When designing enterprise-grade AI agent systems.
## Examples & Case Studies
### Navan adopting cloud runtime environments and building custom rehydration layers.
- **Illustrates**: Bridging the gap between stateless cloud infrastructure and stateful agent requirements.
- **Lesson**: Enterprise requirements demand custom solutions where cloud providers fall short.
## Actionable Takeaways
- **Immediate**:
  - Adopt progressive disclosure for context management.
  - Implement OTEL tracing for agent tool calls and reasoning chains.
- **Strategic**:
  - Start with single-agent architectures with subskills before moving to multi-agent networks.
  - Establish strict guardrails and scoped credentials for tool execution.
- **Questions to investigate**:
  - How do we establish deterministic testing for non-deterministic agents?
  - What standardized trace format will the industry converge upon?
## Claims Worth Verifying
- Model Context Protocol (MCP) has emerged as a de facto protocol for tool calling. (industry trend)
- Trajectory evals are necessary to evaluate multi-step agent success. (architectural best practice)
## Notable Quotes
> "If you can't build a well-structured monolith, what makes you think microservices is the answer?" (at 0:40)
> "We know what's needed. Most of it exists. Go build the rest." (at 31:42)
## Compressed Summary
- Agents mirror microservices in 2015 by facing maturity, observability, and testing challenges.
- A reference architecture spans runtime, memory, skills, observability, testing, guardrails, and orchestration.
- Memory is not just retrieval; it requires multi-tiered short-term, long-term, and episodic storage.
- Single agents with subskills are recommended over complex multi-agent setups initially to avoid cascading failures.
- **Keywords**: agents, microservices, architecture, observability, memory
- **Core insight**: AI agents are currently experiencing the same architectural growing pains as microservices in 2015, requiring disciplined layering in runtime, memory, observability, and guardrails to succeed in enterprise production.
